A variant of the category of [[French drip coffee pot]]s is the group of so-called '''Bohemian coffee pots'''<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20230108210616/https://www.zeller.de/de/suchergebnisse-alle-kataloge/auktionsartikel/karlsbader-kaffeekanne/ Bohemia, 1840 -->,<ref name="Ukers_1922"/><ref name="Ukers_1930"/> manual [[zero-bypass coffee brewing|zero-bypass]] [[flat-bottom coffee filter|flat bottom]] coffee makers made out of [[porcelain]] only, including '''Karlsbad<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20231229122707/https://www.sampor.de/assets/images/alles-aus-papier/preislisten/pl_karlsbader_kaffeemaschine_01a.jpg --> coffee makers''' (1878),<ref name="Thun_1878"/><ref name="Thun_1882"/><ref name="Thun_1895"/><ref name="Thun_AT189x"/><ref name="Thun_HU1897"/><ref name="Ukers_1935"/><ref name="Guggenbichler_200x"/><ref name="Stroessenreuther_2012"/><ref name="Schreibelmayer_2014"/><ref group="nb" name="NB_First_Patent"/> '''Bayreuth coffee makers'''<!-- forms 699-035, 699-070 --> (2007),<ref name="Walküre_2011_1"/><ref name="Schreibelmayer_2014"/><ref name="Walküre_2017"/><ref group="nb" name="NB_Name_Bayreuth"/> {{anchor|Form 799}}the '''Walküre cup filter'''<!-- form 799-020, 200 mL --> (2010)<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20230603194804/https://www.kurier.de/inhalt.bayreuth-ein-filter-fuer-die-kaffeeverrueckten.6ef62717-2b53-4659-a666-46fb83267c58.html --><ref name="Walküre_2011_2"/><ref name="Walküre_2017"/>{{rp|page=128}} and {{anchor|Form 999}}the '''Walküre aroma-pot'''<!-- form 999-035, 350 mL --> (2015)<!-- by Daniel Eltner & Goran Huber for Walküre. A gold version: https://web.archive.org/web/20230107214904/https://ottencoffee.co.id/pour-over/walkure-aroma-pot-gold -->.<ref name="Siemen_1999"/><ref name="HD_2016"/><ref name="FAQ_2016"/><ref name="Walküre_2017"/><ref name="Huber_201x"/><ref group="nb" name="NB_Karlsbad_Tea"/> In contrast to French drip coffee pots, they all use a special double-layered [[conical]]ly cross-slit strainer made from through-[[glaze (painting technique)|glaze]]d porcelain<ref name="Ukers_1922"/><ref name="Rosenthal_Karlsbader"/><ref name="Rosenthal_Cup-filter"/><ref name="Schreibelmayer_2014"/> as well as a water spreader with six<!-- for SPM/Walküre. Hutschenreuther has only 5 --> (or, in the larger models, more) large round holes<ref group="nb" name="NB_Karlsbad_Origin"/> to ensure an even water distribution and reduce the agitation of the [[coffee bed]], a method sometimes also called [[cake filtration (coffee)|cake filtration]]. In particular before [[World War I]], but still up to the advent of the [[Espresso machine]] in the 1950s, they were very popular in the [[Viennese coffee house culture]].<ref name="Bauscher_Hutschenreuther"/><ref name="Singer_1959"/><ref name="Pauzenberger_2009"/><ref name="Freiberger_2012"/><ref name="Wolfschluckner_2014"/><ref name="Broy_2015"/> The special kind of drip coffee they produce is called a {{lang|de|Karlsbader}} ({{gloss|Karlsbad coffee}}).<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20230529094244/https://www.sampor.de/index.php?id=4150 --><ref name="Rosenthal_Karlsbader"/><ref name="Gloess-Schönbächler-Klopprogge-DAmbrosio-Chatelain-Bongartz-Strittmatter-Rast-Yeretzian_2013"/><ref name="Broy_2015"/><ref name="Maltoni-Carli_2020"/><ref group="nb" name="NB_Karlsbad_coffee"/> In Vienna, the {{lang|de-AT|Kleiner Schwarzer}} (confusingly also called {{lang|de-AT|Mokka}} or {{lang|de-AT|Piccolo}}), a black coffee without milk or sugar, was often prepared in Karlsbad coffee makers as well,<ref name="Pauzenberger_2009"/><!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20240323165841/https://kaffee.org/wiener-kaffee-die-kaffeehauskultur-oesterreichs --> hence they were sometimes incorrectly also called '''Vienna coffee-making machines'''.<ref name="Ukers_1922"/><ref name="Ukers_1930"/><ref name="Ukers_1935"/><ref group="nb" name="NB_Vienna_coffee_maker"/> Once manufactured by many porcelain manufacturers, demand gradually dropped and eventually production stopped when [[electrical coffee maker]]s became more and more common, so that Karlsbad coffee makers were only available on the [[used market]] for a couple of decades.<ref name="Guggenbichler_200x"/> However, experiencing a renaissance since about the millennium as part of the so-called [[third-wave of coffee]] one manufacturer restarted production of them.<ref name="Walküre_2002"/><ref name="Guggenbichler_200x"/><ref name="Schreibelmayer_2014"/><ref name="Scholz_2019"/> They are also used in [[restaurant]]s and by [[connoisseur]]s, [[coffee sommelier]]s, [[coffee roaster]]s and in [[coffee tasting]] laboratories.<ref name="Edelbauer_2000"/><ref name="Walküre_2002"/><ref name="Schreibelmayer_2014"/><ref name="Scholz_2019"/>

==History==
{{anchor|Thun}}As a product of the [[fin de siècle]]<ref name="Guggenbichler_200x"/> the original so-called {{lang|de|Karlsbader Kaffeemaschine}} ({{gloss|Karlsbad coffee maker}}) was invented by {{ill|Oswald von Thun und Hohenstein (1849–1913)|de|Oswald von Thun und Hohenstein (Industrieller, 1849)|lt=Oswald von Thun und Hohenstein's}} factory [[Thun'sche Porzellanfabrik]] of {{lang|de|[[Klösterle an der Eger]]}} (now {{lang|cs|Klášterec nad Ohří}}) near {{lang|de|[[Karlsbad (Bohemia)|Karlsbad]]}} (now {{lang|cs|Karlovy Vary}}),<ref name="Schneider_1880"/><ref name="Daheim_1905"/><ref name="Daheim_1906"/><ref name="Sprechsaal_1906"/><ref name="Thun_19xx"/><ref name="KR_1920"/><ref name="Fischer_1984"/><!-- Fischer even mentions coffee makers in 1850, but not Karlsbad-style ones. A Karlsbad-style coffee maker is pictured manufactured by Union-Porzellan since 1900. --> which patented a special cross-slit filter sieve in 1878.<ref name="Thun_1878"/><ref name="Thun_1882"/><ref name="Thun_1895"/><ref name="Thun_AT189x"/><ref name="Thun_HU1897"/><ref name="Ukers_1935"/><ref name="Stroessenreuther_2012"/><ref group="nb" name="NB_First_Patent"/> Producing [[lithophane]]s, the company, which was founded in 1793/1794, already had experience manufacturing very thin and fragile porcelain for decades.<ref name="Schneibergová_2006"/>

Karlsbad coffee makers were historically manufactured by many [[porcelain manufacturer]]s including [[Porcelánka Thun]] (with [[porcelain mark]] "TK") ([[Karlsbad (Bohemia)|Karlsbad]]),<ref name="Schneider_1880"/><ref name="Daheim_1905"/><ref name="Daheim_1906"/><ref name="Sprechsaal_1906"/><ref name="Thun_19xx"/><ref name="Fischer_1984"/><ref name="Stroessenreuther_2012"/> Altrohlauer Porzellan-Fabriken AG vorm. {{ill|Moritz Zdekauer|cs}} ("M Z") ({{ill|Stará Role|de|Altrohlau|lt=Altrohlau}}), {{ill|EPIAG|de|Steingutfabrik Dallwitz|lt=Erste Porzellan-Industrie A.G.}} ("EPIAG D. F.") ([[Dallwitz (Karlsbad District)|Dallwitz]]), {{ill|Georg Haas von Hasenfels|de|lt=Haas}} & {{ill|Johann Czjzek von Smidaich|de|lt=Czjzek}} ("H. & C.") Karlsbad coffee makers consist of four parts (a coffee pot, a coffee strainer/filter, a water spreader/distributor, and a lid) all made out of porcelain,<ref name="Edelbauer_2000"/>{{rp|page=20}} and they exist in a number of different shapes of unknown origin. The original shape appears to have been a cylindrical filter with two squarish handles combined with a ball-shaped pot.<ref name="Siemen_1999"/> Another early style featured a somewhat trapezoid shape known as {{lang|de|neukonisch}} ({{gloss|neoconic}}).<ref name="Maltoni-Carli_2020"/>

{{anchor|Form 523}}In 1910<!-- 1910–1940 -->, SPM incorporated the slit Karlsbad filter into the design of a coffee maker with cylindrical filter (form 523). {{anchor|Form 599}}In 1913<!-- 1913–1942 -->, SPM introduced the now classical somewhat pear-shaped rounded form (form 599)<!-- old sizes: 599/1 = 1.8l, 599/2, 599/3, 599/4, 599/5, 599/6, 599/7; modern sizes: 599-028, 599-038, 599-085, 599-115 -->.<ref name="Siemen_1999"/><ref name="Walküre_2017"/><ref group="nb" name="NB_Karlsbad_Origin"/> This design was copied by other porcelain manufacturers. Over the years it was available in various sizes ranging from <!--there even was a "form-599"-shaped size 8 with reportedly 1/8 L (1 cup) by an unidentified manufacturer - not SPM/Walküre/Friesland -->250 ml<ref name="FPM_2021"/>{{rp|page=30}} to 2.25 litre<!-- originally about 8 different sizes with some variations between manufacturers, Walküre in the 2010s up to 2019 four sizes: 280 mL, 380 mL, 850 mL, 1150 mL. Walküre-Bayreuth Bavaria" -->

[[File:Porzellanfabrik Walküre (01).jpg|thumb|[[Porzellanfabrik Walküre]] at Gravenreutherstraße in [[Bayreuth]], Germany (2014)]]
{{anchor|Form 699}}In 2007, the so-called Bayreuth coffee makers<ref group="nb" name="NB_Name_Bayreuth"/> were created by designer Daniel Eltner for Walküre. A somewhat [[Bauhaus]]-reminiscing slick modernized style (form 699) following the same general four-piece porcelain construction principles as traditional Karlsbad coffee makers, the design received the "[[Good Design Award (Museum of Modern Art)|Good Design Award]] 2008" of the [[Chicago Athenaeum Museum of Architecture and Design]] and the "Coffee Innovations Award 2008" in the category "coffee machines and mills" at the domotechnica fair in Cologne.<ref name="Walküre_2011_1"/><ref name="Walküre_2017"/> However, due to its non-symmetrical design it may be difficult to handle for [[left-hander]]s. It has been available in two sizes (350 ml<!-- form 699-035, decors: white, red, gold --> and 700 ml<!-- form 699-070 -->)<ref name="Walküre_2017"/>{{rp|page=123}} produced by Walküre up to 2019,<ref name="Walküre_2017"/><ref name="Hack_2019"/><ref name="Scholz_2019"/><ref name="BT_2019"/><ref name="Schreibelmayer_2019"/><ref name="Schreibelmayer_2020_1"/><ref name="Gütling_2020"/> and since 2020 by Friesland (400 ml and 700 ml).<ref name="Schreibelmayer_2020_2"/><ref name="FPM_2020"/><ref name="FPM_2021"/>{{rp|page=35}}<ref name="Börjes-Meinardus_2023_2"/>

{{As of|2020}},<ref name="FPM_2020"/><ref name="FPM_2021"/> Friesland was the only remaining manufacturer of any of them; however, their Varel production site burnt down in a fire on 29 June 2023,<ref name="dpa_2023"/><ref name="NDR_2023"/><ref name="Nonstop_2023"/> {{As of|alt=now|October 2024}} pending its reconstruction.<ref name="Börjes-Meinardus_2023"/><ref name="Friesland_2023"/><ref name="Meyer_2023"/><ref name="Börjes-Meinardus_2024"/>

== Preparation ==
To avoid clogging, coarsely ground coffee with about salt- or sugar-sized grains (about [[semolina]]-grade<ref name="Mayerhofer_1931"/><ref name="Walküre_2002"/><ref name="Walküre_2004"/>{{rp|pages=2, 4}}<ref name="Guggenbichler_200x"/><ref name="Walküre_2011_1"/>{{rp|page=133}}<ref name="Töpfer_2016"/><ref name="Walküre_2017"/>{{rp|page=125}}), evenly ground and without [[fines (coffee)|fines]] or added [[coffee surrogate]]s,<ref name="PR_1932"/> has to be used.<ref name="Kolschitzky_2013"/> Walküre recommended to use [[coffea arabica]], and either 16 g for the first two cups and 6 g for each further cup,<ref name="Edelbauer_2000"/>{{rp|page=21}}<ref name="Walküre_2004"/>{{rp|page=4}} or 8–10 g per cup in general.<ref name="Walküre_2011_1"/>{{rp|page=133}}<ref name="Walküre_2017"/>{{rp|page=125}}<!-- <ref name="Freiberger_2012"/> -->

The parts were available in different sizes<!-- at least #1 and #2 --> in white and brown.]]

== Similar coffee makers ==
{{anchor|Thürmer}}In the 1880s,<ref name="Thürmer_1887"/> Max Thürmer, a coffee roaster of [[Dresden]]<!-- Pfotenhauerstraße 8, Falkenstraße 7, Wittenbergerstraße 9, Weisseritzstraße 64 -->, Germany, founded in 1879, advertised Karlsbad coffee and somewhat later also coffee makers (of unknown type) in various newspapers. In the early 1900s, he marketed his own invention of a manual coffee maker (the so-called {{lang|de|Kaffeeaufgußkanne Max Thürmer}}), which, from its outer appearance, looked quite similar to cylindrical Karlsbad coffee makers but featured an air-tight joint (<!-- Wasserverschluß, hydraulischer Verschluß, water seal, water closure, water trap? -->through a lid with a thin film of water) between the permanent filter part and the coffee pot below, and it came with a manual [[valving mechanism]] (by closing the {{ill|spout (teapot)|de|Tülle (Ausguss)|lt=spout}} of the coffee pot) to combine [[coffee steeping|steeping]] (full immersion) with drip-filtering ([[percolation]]).<ref name="Thürmer_1900"/><ref name="Thürmer_19xx"/><ref name="Hauptmann_2001"/>{{rp|page=321}} The devices were manufactured by [[Villeroy & Boch]] for him.<ref name="Thürmer_1903"/> While the permanent filter in early of his devices still featured <!-- 157 -->round drilled holes<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20240101192430/https://www.kleinanzeigen.de/s-anzeige/porzellan-keramik-kaffeefilter-max-thuermer-dresden-drp-119723/2546253902-240-15740 --> like in French drip coffee makers, later units used a double-layered cross-slit filter construction similar to that found in Karlsbad coffee makers, but deliberately with a much coarser grid<!-- with 25 slits effectively forming around 50 holes https://web.archive.org/web/20240101162844/https://www.sampor.de/assets/images/getraenke-und-co/kaffeemaschinen/kaffeefiltriermaschine_03b.jpg -->, with a large air gap between the layers, and using ceramics instead of porcelain<!-- and presumably also not through-glazed -->.<ref name="Thürmer_1900"/><ref name="Thürmer_1903"/><ref name="Thürmer_19xx"/><ref name="Sakowski_2023"/><ref group="nb" name="NB_Thürmer_Dresden"/>

{{anchor|Meißen}}Around 1900<!-- exact date unknown, in the "Knauf period" -->, the [[Staatliche Porzellanmanufaktur Meißen]] of [[Meißen]], Germany, manufactured <!-- tea? -->cup filters utilizing a double-layered radially slit<!-- 2+16+24 slits arranged in the center plus two rings effectively forming 84 holes --> porcelain filter construction much coarser than in Karlsbad coffee makers.<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20240923225317/https://www.ebay.de/itm/374434074524 -->

Since 1926, the idea to combine steeping with drip-filtering was also utilized by [[Berlin]]-based coffee roaster [[Carl Artur<!-- also written as Arthur --> Büttner]] in his invention of a manual coffee maker.<ref name="Velten_2018"/> While his construction was considerably different, it also featured a valving mechanism (through a rotatable [[saucer]]), a through-glazed porcelain filter with triangularly-arranged slits and with an air space below.<ref name="Büttner_1928"/><ref name="Büttner_1931"/><ref name="Büttner_1932"/><ref name="Büttner_1933"/><ref name="Büttner_1935"/> These so-called [["System Büttner" coffee maker]]s were available up into, at least, the 1940s<!-- TBD theoretically possible up into the 1960s --> as stand-alone devices for home use, but were also adopted by various other German coffee roasters as part of larger coffee machines produced by the porcelain manufacturer {{ill|Bauscher (company)|de|Bauscher|lt=Bauscher}} for heavy-duty [[coffee batch brew|batch use]] in [[restaurant]]s and [[canteen (cafeteria)|canteen]]s.

Since c. 1952<!-- tea percolators "Aromat" since 1950, coffee percolators since 1952, renamed "Aromator" in 1953 --> (and up into the 1970s) the Neuerer Porzellanfabrik in [[Oberkotzau]], Germany, the successor of Porzellanfabrik Greiner & Herda, manufactured [[coffee percolator]]s named [[Aromator]], which featured double-layered cross-slit <!-- probably not through-glazed? -->porcelain filters similar to those used in Karlsbad coffee makers,<ref name="Neuerer_1964"/><ref name="Aromator"/> and thus not requiring any [[paper filter ring]]s.

{{anchor|RS16|Pure Over}}Modern manual coffee makers sometimes associated with Karlsbad-style coffee makers include Coffee Consulate's intense extraction cup filter ''RS16 GlasFilter'' by Steffen Schwarz (2015)<!-- RS16 GlasFilter, RS16 MetalFilter, RS16 POMFilter, RS16 Tritan, RS40 POMFilter. 16 g very coarsly ground coffee, 200 mL water, 20-30 s blooming, 2 pours, 3-5 minutes drip time. https://web.archive.org/web/20230923131642/https://www.wholelattecoffee.com/2015/10/review-coffee-consulate-rs-16/ https://web.archive.org/web/20240108212021/https://www.kaffee-netz.de/threads/porzellanfabrik-walkuere-geschlossen-das-aus-fuer-die-karlsbader-kanne.129302/ https://web.archive.org/web/20240108201445/https://www.amazon.de/Kaffeebereiter-Intense-Extraction-Filter-Tassenauflage/dp/B00K5Q3UUQ/ref=cm_cr_arp_d_product_top?ie=UTF8 --><ref group="nb" name="NB_RS16"/> and the [[borosilicate]] carafe coffee maker "''The Pure Over''" by [[glass artist]] Etai Rahmil (2020).<!-- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXAQokO-ROE https://web.archive.org/web/20240406145039/https://pureover.com/ --> However, whilst they are zero-bypass flat-bottom French drip coffee pots with [[permanent coffee filter|permanent filter]]s, they too cannot be counted as Karlsbad-style coffee makers because they do not feature a cross-slit double-layered filter sieve and also because they are not made out of porcelain.

{{r|group="nb"|name="NB_Karlsbad_coffee"|r={{anchor|Coffee spices}}Historically, three types of coffee appear to have been referred to as {{lang|de|Karlsbader}} ({{gloss|Karlsbad coffee}}). Weber|de}}, {{ill|Heinrich Franck Söhne|de|Heinrich Franck Söhne|lt=Heinrich Franck & Söhne}} (Kagold), Andre Hofer, Gebrüder Bernhard, {{ill|Kaiser's Kaffee|de}} and others, the second one a drip coffee prepared in a Karlsbad coffee maker, and the third one a combination of both.<!-- <ref name="Maltoni-Carli_2020"/> --> At least in Vienna, coffee, including Karlsbad coffee, appears to have been traditionally served with a slight amount of [[fig coffee]] added.<!-- <ref name="Singer_1959"/>{{rp|page=104}} -->}}

{{r|group="nb"|name="NB_First_Patent"|r={{anchor|Patent}}In Germany ({{lang|de|[[Deutsches Kaiserreich]]}}), the first public patent office ({{lang|de|Kaiserliches Patentamt}} in Berlin) opened on 1 July 1877, replacing various<!-- 25 --> local [[small state]] patent regulations.<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20240929122535/https://www.dpma.de/docs/dpma/veroeffentlichungen/140jahredpma.pdf --> Just a few months later, the [[K. K. Priv. Graf Oswald von Thun'sche Porcellanfabrik]] filed their [[#DE3105|patent 3105]] on the manufacturing of conically cross-slit through-glazed porcelain coffee filters on 5 April 1878<!-- <ref name="Thun_1878"/><ref name="Ukers_1935"/> -->. Given that patents were still very new, it is possible that such filters had been produced for a couple of years earlier already. When other manufacturers later produced similar coffee makers, Thun advertised their coffee makers as the original Karlsbad coffee makers, suggesting that they were actually the first to manufacture them.<!-- <ref name="KR_1920"/><ref name="Ukers_1935"/> --> In Austria ({{lang|de|K.&K. Monarchie Österreich-Ungarn}}), the first patent office opened in 1899<!-- first patent law in 1897 -->, replacing various forms of privileges since 1794.<!-- https://web.archive.org/web/20220808003108/https://www.patentamt.at/alle-news/news-detail/artikel/als-gnadenakte-aus-der-mode-kamen/ -->}}

extract: A variant of the category of French drip coffee pots is the group of so-called Bohemian coffee pots, manual zero-bypass flat bottom coffee makers made out of porcelain only, including Karlsbad coffee makers (1878), Bayreuth coffee makers (2007), the Walküre cup filter (2010) and the Walküre aroma-pot (2015). In contrast to French drip coffee pots, they all use a special double-layered conically cross-slit strainer made from through-glazed porcelain as well as a water spreader with six (or, in the larger models, more) large round holes to ensure an even water distribution and reduce the agitation of the coffee bed, a method sometimes also called cake filtration. In particular before World War I, but still up to the advent of the Espresso machine in the 1950s, they were very popular in the Viennese coffee house culture. The special kind of drip coffee they produce is called a Karlsbader ('Karlsbad coffee'). In Vienna, the Kleiner Schwarzer (confusingly also called Mokka or Piccolo), a black coffee without milk or sugar, was often prepared in Karlsbad coffee makers as well, hence they were sometimes incorrectly also called Vienna coffee-making machines. Once manufactured by many porcelain manufacturers, demand gradually dropped and eventually production stopped when electrical coffee makers became more and more common, so that Karlsbad coffee makers were only available on the used market for a couple of decades. However, experiencing a renaissance since about the millennium as part of the so-called third-wave of coffee one manufacturer restarted production of them. They are also used in restaurants and by connoisseurs, coffee sommeliers, coffee roasters and in coffee tasting laboratories.
